aab.title: How to Build an Approval Workflow
aab.desc: Map the request, the approvers, and the rules once, and Emergent generates the request form, the routing, the alerts, and the audit log around them. Seven steps from the first request to a workflow your team actually uses.
steps: 01 Choose how you will build it

Approvals usually live in email chains, spreadsheets, per-seat approval tools, or workflow suites. Email and spreadsheets leave no audit trail, and per-seat tools charge for every occasional approver. Emergent generates the form, the routing, and the audit log in one build, with every approver included.
02 Define the trigger and the request

Name what starts the approval: a submitted form, an uploaded invoice, an inbound email, or a deal change in HubSpot. The trigger decides the request fields, such as amount, vendor, department, category, and the documents a reviewer needs to decide without asking.
03 Write the approval matrix

Write who approves what, and in what order: under $500 to the manager, $500 to $5,000 to the department head, above that to the CFO, with legal in parallel for contracts. Written as plain sentences, the matrix becomes the routing logic.
04 Set escalation and fallback rules

Decide what happens when an approver goes quiet: a reminder after one business day, escalation to their manager after two, and a fallback approver when someone is out of office. The SLAs you set here decide your cycle time more than any other rule.
05 Choose where approvers decide

Put approve and reject where approvers already work: Slack, Microsoft Teams, or email, with the full request context in the message. Every decision writes back to the workflow, so nobody logs in to a separate portal to clear a queue.
06 Decide what the audit log records

Record the requester, approver chain, amount, decision, reason, and time to approve for every request. On Emergent the log is a database table you own, so finance and audit query it directly, and a dashboard shows cycle time by approver.
07 Pilot with one team, then roll out

Turn it on for one team, run real requests through it for two weeks, and read time to approve from the audit log. Tighten the rules and SLAs by prompting, then roll it out to the next department, with every version kept in exportable code.

sqb.title: How to Create a Customer Satisfaction Survey
sqb.desc: Pick the metric, tie every answer to the customer, and route low scores to someone who can act. Emergent generates the survey, the follow-ups, the alerts, and the dashboard from one description, with no response cap.
steps: 01 Decide what you are measuring

Use CSAT right after a transaction, NPS for loyalty over time, and CES for the effort of a single interaction. Pick one headline metric per survey; asking all three at once costs completions before it adds insight.
02 Pick the moment you ask

Send it where the experience just happened: on ticket close, seven days after delivery, at day 30 of onboarding, or at quarter end for B2B accounts. A survey tied to a real moment gets more responses than a long one sent weeks later.
03 Write the questions and follow-ups

Pair the score with one question about why, one segmentation field such as plan or role, and one improvement question. Branch by score: promoters get a review request, passives a feature question, and detractors an open follow-up.
04 Tie every response to the customer

Pass the customer ID, account, plan, order, or ticket ID with the survey link, so every answer is saved with its context. Without it, a low score is an anonymous number. With it, it is an account someone can call today.
05 Route low scores to an owner

Decide who hears about which score: a Slack alert to the CSM on every detractor, a HubSpot task on a low CSAT, an email to the account owner for key accounts. Every alert should carry the score, the comment, and the customer.
06 Generate the survey and dashboard

Emergent generates the survey, the branching, the alerts, and a live CSAT, NPS, and CES dashboard, all reading from a response database you own. Embed it in your app or emails, or share it on your own domain.
07 Close the loop every week

Read the dashboard weekly by segment and product area, follow up on every detractor within a day, and tell customers what changed because of their feedback. Adjust the questions and thresholds by prompting as patterns appear.

lp.title: How to Build a Thank You Page
lp.desc: A thank you page confirms the action, delivers the promise, and moves the visitor to one next step. Describe what it follows and Emergent generates the page, the database write, and the conversion tracking, on your domain.
steps: 01 Name the action it follows

Start with what the visitor just did: submitted a form, bought a product, registered for a webinar, or booked a call. The action decides the confirmation copy, what gets delivered on the page, and the natural next step.
02 Confirm the action in one line

Say plainly that it worked and what happens next, such as your playbook arriving in two minutes or order #10482 shipping Tuesday. A specific confirmation stops the refresh and resubmit that creates duplicate leads and orders.
03 Deliver the promise on the page

Put the download, the order summary, the calendar link, or the booking time on the page itself, not only in a follow-up email. The visitor gets what they came for immediately, and the email becomes a backup instead of a dependency.
04 Offer one next step

Pick one: book a demo after a lead magnet, add a related product after a purchase, or invite a colleague after a webinar registration. One clear next step converts better than a page crowded with options.
05 Save every visitor and fire the tracking

Write each conversion to a database you own with UTMs, source, and referrer, and fire the GA4 event and Meta Pixel on load. The page becomes a measurable conversion goal and a retargeting audience from the first visit.
06 Publish on your domain

Connect your domain, set the page to noindex, and point the form, checkout, or booking redirect at the new URL. It works as a custom thank you page for WooCommerce or Shopify, a WordPress form redirect, or any standalone form.
07 Test the next step and iterate
Generate an A/B variant of the next-step block by prompting, compare next-step conversion by traffic source every week, keep the winner, and change the offer as your campaigns change.

form.title: How to Build a Creator Application Form
form.desc: Decide who belongs in the program, then let the form do the first round of screening. Emergent generates the application form, the fit scoring, the review queue, and the creator database from one description.
steps: 01 Define who the program is for

Decide who should apply: brand ambassadors from your customer base, UGC creators for paid content, affiliates on commission, or content creators for a role. Each program asks different questions, so settle this before the first field.
02 Set your fit criteria

Decide what makes a creator a fit: follower range, engagement rate, niche, audience region, content style, and rates for paid work. These criteria become both the form fields and the scoring model, so keep every one measurable.
03 Ask platform-specific questions

Show TikTok, Instagram, or YouTube questions only when a creator selects that platform, with one section per channel for multi-platform creators. Keep the whole form to around ten fields; every extra question costs completions.
04 Collect samples and media kits

Accept portfolio links, video samples, and media kit PDFs in the same form, stored with each application. Reviewers see the work next to the numbers instead of opening links from a spreadsheet one by one.
05 Score applications on arrival

Score each application against your criteria the moment it is submitted. Creators above the bar land in an approve queue, borderline ones in a review list, and the rest get a waitlist or decline email without anyone sending it by hand.
06 Automate what happens on approval

Approved creators get the next step automatically: a contract to sign, a referral code or tracked affiliate link, a product seeding request, or a Slack post to your team. Every status change writes to a creator database you own.
07 Publish and review the shortlist

Put the form on your domain, embed it on your creator page, or link it from your bio. Applications arrive scored, so reviewers work from a shortlist and adjust thresholds by prompting as the program grows.
